summary: Defines a Proxy Mobile IPv6 mobility option for negotiating GRE encapsulation and exchanging GRE keys, used to mark upstream and downstream traffic for a mobility session. It can also negotiate GRE without keys. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a mobile node is away from its home network, its traffic is tunnelled between a router at the edge of the visited network and a router in the home network. If two visited networks use the same private address ranges, the two ends cannot tell whose traffic is whose. This RFC adds a number to each tunnel packet that says which session it belongs to.

The two routers agree on the numbers in the messages they already use to set up the session.

questions: what is the gre key option
subtitle: A number in every tunnelled packet that says which mobile session it belongs to.

tldr.problem: The tunnel between a visited network and a home network carries a mobile node's traffic, but the IPv6 and IPv4 encapsulation modes of Proxy Mobile IPv6 cannot always tell the packets of one session from the packets of another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a GRE Key option to the Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement messages. The two ends negotiate GRE encapsulation and exchange a pair of 32-bit keys, one for each direction, which are then put in the GRE header of every tunnelled packet.
tldr.outcome: The receiver can tell which mobility session an arriving packet belongs to, which matters when two operators use overlapping private address space. The document is a Proposed Standard and does not change anything for IPv4 or IPv6 mobile nodes.

facts.label: Next Header for a GRE header

today: RFC 5845 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It extends Proxy Mobile IPv6, defined in RFC 5213, with a new mobility option for negotiating GRE encapsulation and exchanging GRE keys. The IPv4 side of Proxy Mobile IPv6 comes from RFC 5844.

sections.title: Why GRE Keys in Proxy Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
The Proxy Mobile IPv6 specification and IPv4 Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6 allow the IPv6 and IPv4 encapsulation modes for the tunnel between the local mobility anchor (LMA) and the mobile access gateway (MAG). In some scenarios those encapsulation modes are not enough to identify uniquely the destination of the packets of a particular mobility session, so an encapsulation mode with richer semantics is needed. Generic Routing Encapsulation, with the Key extension, has the semantics that allow such a distinction.

This document defines the GRE Key option, which is used to negotiate GRE encapsulation mode and to exchange the uplink and downlink GRE keys. The negotiated keys can be used to mark the downlink and uplink traffic of a specific mobility session. The document also lets the two ends negotiate GRE encapsulation mode without exchanging any keys.

It has no impact on IPv4 or IPv6 mobile nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: When a mobile node is away from its home network, its traffic is tunnelled between a router at the edge of the visited network and a router in the home network. If two visited networks use the same private address ranges, the two ends cannot tell whose traffic is whose. This RFC adds a number to each tunnel packet that says which session it belongs to.

sections.title: Downlink, Uplink and the Two GRE Keys
sections.content:
The RFC uses four terms. Downlink traffic is the traffic in the tunnel between the local mobility anchor and the mobile access gateway that heads towards the mobile access gateway and is tunnelled at the local mobility anchor. It is also called forward direction traffic. Uplink traffic is the traffic in the same tunnel that heads towards the local mobility anchor and is tunnelled at the mobile access gateway. It is also called reverse direction traffic.

The downlink GRE key is assigned by the mobile access gateway and used by the local mobility anchor to mark the downlink traffic that belongs to a specific mobility session. The uplink GRE key is assigned by the local mobility anchor and used by the mobile access gateway to mark the uplink traffic that belongs to a specific mobility session.

A policy check is what the local mobility anchor does when it receives an initial binding lifetime extension, or a binding lifetime extension proxy binding update for a mobility session: it decides whether GRE encapsulation mode only, or GRE encapsulation with GRE keys, is required. That policy could be per MAG and LMA pair, a local policy of the anchor, a policy per mobile node, or any combination of these.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic towards the mobile node and traffic away from it each get their own number, and each number is chosen by the router that sends that direction. The anchor decides, case by case, whether the numbers are needed at all.

sections.title: GRE Encapsulation and the Overlapping Address Problem
sections.content:
With the GRE Key option, the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor can negotiate GRE encapsulation mode only, in which case no GRE keys are used at all, or GRE encapsulation mode with the exchange of the GRE keys. Once the keys have been exchanged, the mobile access gateway puts the uplink key, assigned by the local mobility anchor, in the GRE header of the uplink payload packet, and the local mobility anchor puts the downlink key, negotiated with the mobile access gateway, in the GRE header of the downlink payload packet.

Figure 1 of the RFC shows the case this solves. A local mobility anchor provides mobility service to mobile nodes from different operators, and those mobile nodes have been assigned IPv4 addresses from overlapping private address space. Operator-A and Operator-B both use 10.x.0.0/16. The mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor have to be able to distinguish the flows that belong to each operator, so they exchange a specific pair of downlink and uplink GRE keys and save them as part of the mobile node's binding.

With those keys, the anchor and the gateway can tell the flows of each mobile node apart by the GRE key in the header of the tunnelled payload packet, and route them accordingly. The RFC notes one limit: the keys apply to the individual mobility binding updated by the proxy binding update, and not to all the bindings a mobile node may have registered under the procedures of RFC 5648.
sections.plainLanguage: Two operators can both use the same private address ranges for their mobile users. The GRE key tells the two ends which operator's traffic a packet belongs to, so the packets are routed to the right place.

sections.title: Negotiating Encapsulation and Exchanging Keys
sections.content:
To ask for GRE encapsulation mode only, without any keys, the mobile access gateway MUST include the GRE Key option but omit the GRE Key Identifier field in the Proxy Binding Update. If the anchor supports GRE encapsulation and the update contains the option without the identifier, the anchor reads that as a request for GRE encapsulation without dynamic key exchange, and, if it processes the update successfully, it answers with a successful Proxy Binding Acknowledgement that carries the option with the identifier omitted.

To ask for GRE encapsulation with keys, the gateway MUST include the GRE Key option in the initial Proxy Binding Update and MUST put the downlink GRE key in the GRE Key Identifier field. When the anchor has processed the update successfully and has accepted both the encapsulation request and the downlink key after a policy check, it MUST include the GRE Key option with the uplink GRE key in the identifier field of a successful Proxy Binding Acknowledgement.

Once the keys have been exchanged for a mobility session, the anchor MUST keep the same negotiated uplink GRE key for the lifetime of that session, although for administrative reasons, such as a reboot, it MAY change it, in which case some packet loss may be experienced. The gateway MUST include the GRE Key option with the downlink key in the Proxy Binding Update that asks for a binding lifetime extension, and the anchor MUST answer with the same uplink key it gave last time for that session.

During a handoff between mobile access gateways, the new gateway MUST include the GRE Key option with the downlink key in the Proxy Binding Update that asks for the after-handoff binding lifetime extension, if it decides that GRE encapsulation and keys are required. It may either pick a new downlink key or use the one the previous gateway used for the same binding; to know that key it may need a transfer of context from the previous gateway, and the RFC leaves that mechanism out of scope. When the anchor processes a handoff-triggered update that carries a downlink key, it MUST answer with the same uplink key it exchanged with the previous gateway for that session.

If the anchor receives a handoff-triggered update without the GRE Key option for a binding that is using GRE keys, it makes a policy check. If the policy says GRE encapsulation and keys are required, the anchor MUST reject the update with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement whose status is GRE_KEY_OPTION_REQUIRED. Otherwise it SHOULD accept the update, and if it processes it successfully it MUST answer with a successful acknowledgement that does not include the option.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree on the tunnel format in the same messages they already use to set up the mobility session. The gateway proposes, the anchor agrees and hands back its own key, and both remember the pair for as long as the session lasts.

sections.title: What Each Side Stores
sections.content:
Every mobile access gateway keeps a Binding Update List entry for each attached mobile node, and this document extends that entry with four fields. A flag says whether GRE encapsulation is enabled for the mobile node's traffic. The downlink GRE key is the key the gateway generated and sent to the anchor in the GRE Key option. The uplink GRE key is the key the gateway took from the identifier field of the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement. A further flag says whether the UDP-based TLV-header format is enabled for the mobile node's traffic, and it is true only when both UDP tunnelling and GRE encapsulation are enabled for the session.

The local mobility anchor keeps a binding cache entry, and this document extends it with the same four fields: the GRE encapsulation flag, the downlink key that the gateway assigned, the uplink key that the anchor assigned, and the flag for the UDP-based TLV-header format.

On receiving a packet from the tunnel with a GRE header, both the gateway and the anchor MUST use the GRE key in the GRE extension header as an additional identifier to work out which mobility session the packet belongs to, and they remove the GRE header before any further processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps the two numbers with the mobile node's session, and when a tunnelled packet arrives the number in its GRE header says which session it belongs to.

sections.title: The GRE Key Option and the Status Codes
sections.content:
The GRE Key option is a new mobility option for the Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages exchanged between the gateway and the anchor. It can be used to negotiate GRE encapsulation mode only, or GRE encapsulation with the exchange of the keys, and the keys can then be used in all the GRE encapsulated payload packets to mark the traffic of that specific mobile node. The alignment requirement for the option is 4n.

The option has a Type field, whose value is 33, a Length field, a 16-bit Reserved field and a 32-bit GRE Key Identifier field. The Length field gives the length in octets of the option, excluding the Type and Length fields. A value of 2 means the GRE Key Identifier is not carried; a value of 6 means that either the downlink or the uplink key is carried. The Reserved field is unused, and MUST be initialised to zero by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver. The GRE Key Identifier holds the downlink or the uplink key, and is present only when the keys are being exchanged.

Both messages also get a new flag, the TLV-header format flag, shown as the T bit in the Proxy Binding Update and the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement. In the update it says that the gateway requests the TLV header for encapsulating IPv6 or IPv4 packets in IPv4. In the acknowledgement it says that the anchor supports tunnelling IPv6 or IPv4 in IPv4 using the TLV-header format. No other field or flag of either message is changed.

Three status codes are defined for the Binding Acknowledgement message. GRE_KEY_OPTION_NOT_REQUIRED, value 2, means the anchor processed the update successfully but has decided that GRE encapsulation and keys are not required. GRE_TUNNELING_BUT_TLV_HEADER_NOT_SUPPORTED, value 3, means GRE encapsulation was negotiated successfully but the TLV-header format is not supported. GRE_KEY_OPTION_REQUIRED, value 163, rejects the update because the anchor has decided that GRE encapsulation and keys are required.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is small: a type number, a length, and a 32-bit field that holds the key or is left out. The length tells the receiver which of the two cases it is, so the two ends can agree on the format even before any key exists.

sections.title: Data Packets and the TLV Header
sections.content:
When GRE encapsulation is used, the gateway may tunnel the IPv6 or IPv4 payload packet in IPv6 or in IPv4, following the rules of Proxy Mobile IPv6 and of IPv4 Support for Proxy Mobile IPv6. The order of headers for a plain GRE tunnel is an outer IPv6 or IPv4 header, then the GRE header, then the payload, which carries its own IPv6 or IPv4 header.

If UDP-based tunnelling is used together with GRE encapsulation, the TLV-header UDP tunnelling format MUST be used, with the order: IPv4 header, UDP header, TLV header, GRE header, payload, upper layer protocols. The use of the TLV header is negotiated during the Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement exchange. The TLV header holds a Type field, the type of the payload header that follows, and its length. The Type field is always 0, so that the receiver can tell a TLV header from an IP header. That lets the TLV header carry traffic other than IP, as the Next Header field indicates. The distinction matters because the Proxy Binding Update, which is an IP packet, and the data packets, which are GRE packets, can travel over the same UDP tunnel.

The TLV header itself has a Type byte that is always 0, a Reserved byte that is unused, a Next Header byte that gives the protocol number of the payload header that follows, and a 16-bit Length field giving the length in octets of the payload that follows, excluding the TLV header. If an IPv6 header follows, the Next Header value should be 41; if a GRE header follows, it should be 47. A receiver that finds the payload length calculated from the UDP header different from the length calculated from the TLV header MUST discard the packet.

The gateway negotiates the tunnelling format during the Proxy Mobile IPv6 registration procedure. If it needs the TLV-header UDP encapsulation format it MUST set the T flag in the Proxy Binding Update, and if the anchor supports it the anchor SHOULD set the flag in the acknowledgement. Otherwise the flag is cleared, and a cleared flag in the acknowledgement tells the gateway that it MUST use the TLV-header UDP encapsulation format for all the packets it tunnels for the whole time the mobile node is attached. The format SHOULD NOT change during a binding lifetime extension from the same gateway. A handoff-triggered update may renegotiate the format, so to avoid interoperability problems the anchor MUST NOT set the T flag unless it was set in the update it received.

If the gateway sees the status GRE_TUNNELING_BUT_TLV_HEADER_NOT_SUPPORTED, it MUST use GRE encapsulation without UDP encapsulation if it is allowed to do so, and set the TLV-header flag to false. Otherwise it may resend the update to negotiate different tunnelling options, such as UDP-based tunnelling without GRE encapsulation, or de-register the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The packets travel in a tunnel whose outer header can be IPv4, UDP, a small type header, GRE and then the user's own packet. The small type header tells the receiver which protocol follows, so the same UDP tunnel can carry both the control messages and the data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The GRE Key option, when carried in Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, reveals the group affiliation of a mobile node identified by its Network Access Identifier or an IP address. That may help an attacker in targeting the flows belonging to a specific group. The vulnerability can be prevented by enabling confidentiality protection on the Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, where the presence of the NAI and GRE Key options establishes a mobile node's relation to a specific group. It can also be avoided by enabling confidentiality protection on all the tunnelled data packets between the gateway and the anchor, so that the markings are hidden.

In Proxy Mobile IPv6 the use of IPsec for protecting a mobile node's data traffic is optional, and Proxy Mobile IPv6 recommends ESP in tunnel mode when ESP is used for that traffic. When GRE encapsulation is used, both IPsec tunnel mode and transport mode can be used to protect the GRE header. The IPsec traffic selectors contain the protocol number for GRE, and there is currently no mechanism to use the GRE key as a traffic selector.
sections.plainLanguage: The key in the packet header tells anyone watching which session a packet belongs to. If that matters, the control messages and the tunnelled data should be encrypted.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The mobility option type. The value for this option is 33.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the option, excluding the Type and Length fields. 2 means no key is carried, 6 means a key is carried.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Unused. Must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: GRE Key Identifier
fields.desc: The downlink or the uplink GRE key, present only when the keys are being exchanged.

items.label: GRE_KEY_OPTION_NOT_REQUIRED
items.desc: The update was processed successfully, but GRE encapsulation and keys are not needed.

items.label: GRE_TUNNELING_BUT_TLV_HEADER_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: GRE encapsulation was agreed, but the TLV-header format is not supported.

items.label: GRE_KEY_OPTION_REQUIRED
items.desc: The update is rejected, because GRE encapsulation and keys are required.

items.title: The problem
items.text: Two operators use the same private address ranges, so the tunnel cannot tell the flows apart.

items.title: The fix
items.text: Each mobility session is given a pair of GRE keys, one for each direction.

items.title: Where the key sits
items.text: In the GRE header of every tunnelled packet.

items.title: What it identifies
items.text: The mobility session the packet belongs to.
